subtopics.title: Newton's second law, force and mass
subtopics.learning_goal: Relate net force, constant mass and acceleration; use the relation in forward and inverse directions without confusing applied and resultant forces.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Distinguish applied from resultant forces; infer one resistance from measured acceleration, then recover the other mass and verify both independently.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: For A, ΣF_A=m_Aa_A=2×3=6 N east. Applied push is 8 N east, so the unknown A resistance is 8−6=2 N west. For B, the independently given resistance is 2 N west; hence ΣF_B=8−2=6 N east. Its mass is m_B=6/1.5=4 kg. The two net forces are equal only after checking the resistances. Verify A: 8−2=2×3=6 N; B: 8−2=4×1.5=6 N.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Infer an unknown mass from equal *net* forces and inverse mass-acceleration proportionality, not by direct forward substitution.

representation_translation.evidence: Two frictionless carts receive the same horizontal constant net force. Cart A has mass 2 kg and acceleration 3 m s⁻² east. Cart B accelerates 1.5 m s⁻² east. Find B's mass without being told the common force directly. Justify the equality you use and check the units.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Equal net forces imply m_A a_A = m_B a_B. So 2 kg×3 m s⁻² = m_B×1.5 m s⁻², giving m_B=4 kg. Independent check: both forces are 6 N east; B's larger mass has smaller acceleration as expected.

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Equal net forces imply m_A a_A = m_B a_B. So 2 kg×3 m s⁻² = m_B×1.5 m s⁻², giving m_B=4 kg. Independent check: both forces are 6 N east; B's larger mass has smaller acceleration as expected.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: The same experiment is repeated, but B now has net friction of 2 N west while the same 6 N east applied force acts on both. What is B's acceleration if its mass is 4 kg?

subtopics.title: Newton's third law and interacting objects
subtopics.learning_goal: Identify genuine interaction pairs on two distinct objects and separate equal contact forces from unequal accelerations.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Separate action-reaction forces by recipient, add each body's external device, then reconcile body equations with the system centre of mass.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: B-on-A contact =−12 N (west); A-on-B contact=+12 N (east). For A, ΣF_A=+4−12=−8 N, so a_A=−8/4=−2 m s⁻². For B, ΣF_B=+12−3=+9 N, so a_B=+9/1=+9 m s⁻². The combined system's external resultant is +4−3=+1 N, total mass 5 kg and a_CM=+1/5=+0.2 m s⁻². Independent check: (4×−2+1×9)/5=+0.2 m s⁻². The contact pair cancels only in the combined system; the opposing accelerations can cause separation soon after this instantaneous snapshot.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Pair forces by interacting bodies first; only then compute separate accelerations from distinct masses.

representation_translation.evidence: During a brief horizontal contact on a smooth track, cart A (4 kg) pushes cart B (1 kg) with force 12 N east. Identify the force on A by B, then compare each cart's instantaneous acceleration due to these contact forces. Explain precisely why unequal accelerations do not contradict Newton's third law.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Force on B by A is +12 N east, while force on A by B is −12 N west. If these are the only horizontal forces during the contact, a_A=−12/4=−3 m s⁻² and a_B=+12/1=+12 m s⁻². Forces are equal and opposite, accelerations differ because masses differ.

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Force on B by A is +12 N east, while force on A by B is −12 N west. If these are the only horizontal forces during the contact, a_A=−12/4=−3 m s⁻² and a_B=+12/1=+12 m s⁻². Forces are equal and opposite, accelerations differ because masses differ.

subtopics.learning_goal: Choose an analysis system, enumerate its external interactions, and infer a previously unlabelled contact force from its acceleration.

subtopics.title: Friction and contact conditions
subtopics.learning_goal: Distinguish adjusting static friction from its limiting value and identify when a proposed static equilibrium becomes impossible.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Apply the static feasibility inequality before and after an external change, then switch to the stated kinetic friction model only if equilibrium fails.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: Initially the nonfriction tendency is +8−3=+5 N east; static friction adjusts to −5 N (5 N west). Since |5|≤6 N, the crate remains at rest. With the rope raised to 16 N west, the nonfriction resultant is +8−16=−8 N (west); rest would require +8 N east static friction, exceeding its 6 N limit. The crate starts sliding west, so 4 N kinetic friction acts east. The actual net is +8−16+4=−4 N, and a=−4/2=−2 m s⁻², i.e. 2 m s⁻² west. Static limit is never substituted as actual kinetic friction.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Compute net impending-slip tendency from multiple applied interactions, then compare the required static friction with its bound.

representation_translation.evidence: A crate initially rests on a level floor. One person pushes east with 8 N while a rope pulls west with 3 N. The maximum static friction is 6 N. Determine whether it stays at rest and find actual friction including direction. Justify why it is not simply the limiting value.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: The nonfriction tendency is +8−3=+5 N east. To remain at rest, static friction must be −5 N, i.e. 5 N west. Its magnitude 5 N is at most the 6 N limit, so rest is possible. The actual friction is 5 N, not 6 N.

algebra_computational_load.evidence: The nonfriction tendency is +8−3=+5 N east. To remain at rest, static friction must be −5 N, i.e. 5 N west. Its magnitude 5 N is at most the 6 N limit, so rest is possible. The actual friction is 5 N, not 6 N.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Now increase the eastward push to 11 N but leave the 3 N west rope and 6 N maximum static friction unchanged. Can the crate remain at rest? What additional information is needed to compute its sliding acceleration?

qrt_targets.protected_work: Test feasibility of static balance before changing to a kinetic contact model, then form the actual signed resultant to obtain acceleration.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: The nonfriction tendency is +7−2=+5 N east. To remain at rest would need 5 N west static friction, exceeding the 4 N maximum, so static equilibrium is impossible. Sliding begins east, hence kinetic friction is −3 N west. The kinetic resultant is 7−2−3=+2 N east. With mass 2 kg, a_x=+2/2=+1 m s⁻². The 4 N limit is a bound on static contact, not the friction used after sliding begins.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Nonfriction tendency=+7−2=+5 N. Static rest requires friction 5 N west, but capacity is 4 N, so rest is impossible in the stated model. To compute sliding acceleration require crate mass and kinetic-friction magnitude/coefficient. One cannot infer acceleration from static maximum alone.

representation_translation.evidence: A crate at rest on a level floor is acted on by 7 N east and 2 N west, with static-friction capacity 4 N. A learner insists the crate remains still because 'static friction is always available'. Determine whether static or sliding contact is the appropriate next model; identify the missing kinetic information needed for acceleration.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Select static equilibrium feasibility by comparing required friction to its physical limit rather than applying an automatic f=μN.

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Select static equilibrium feasibility by comparing required friction to its physical limit rather than applying an automatic f=μN.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: If the westward force were 4 N rather than 2 N, what would actual static friction be?

derivation_steps.why_valid: Newton's first law: in an inertial frame, net force zero implies constant vector velocity. Along one axis, Δv/Δt=0 when ΣF_x=0, and x(t)=x₀+v₀t while this condition holds. Velocity has dimensions m s⁻¹; displacement has dimensions m. A translating, accelerating bus frame is not itself inertial, so distinguish observations from model-based forces.

model_limits: If friction on the suitcase is large enough, its horizontal net force is west during braking, so the suitcase can slow with the bus instead of sliding.
A changed contact condition changes the first-law premise; do not apply ΣF=0 when nonzero friction acts.

progressive_examples.independent_check: With nonzero friction the first-law premise has changed.

misconception.wrong_model: A suitcase is thrown forward by an extra force when a bus brakes.

core1a.phenomenon: Two trolleys receive the same horizontal net push. The lighter trolley changes velocity more quickly, showing that acceleration depends on both resultant force and inertia.
core1a.scientific_narrative: Choose the object, collect its external forces, compute their signed resultant, and only then divide by mass. The applied push is not necessarily the resultant because contact friction or an opposing rope can modify the total. Under the constant-mass Newtonian model, an equal net force produces acceleration inversely proportional to mass. Compare mass and acceleration only when resultant forces are known to be equal. Additional Core1A operation bridges (AUTHOR CANDIDATE, not approved): APPLY: Force can change suddenly while a non-impulsive motion keeps position and velocity continuous. Split time at each force change; calculate ΣF/m for each stage and use the outgoing velocity of one stage as the next stage's initial velocity. For constant acceleration in a stage, v_next=v_start+aΔt and Δx=v_startΔt+½aΔt². Do not reuse the original speed for later stages or add speeds without respecting signs. Different worked example: A 2 kg cart starts with v=1 m s⁻¹ east. A +4 N resultant acts for 1 s, giving a=+2 m s⁻² and v=3 m s⁻¹; the resultant then becomes zero for 2 s, so it coasts 6 m farther at 3 m s⁻¹. Independent check: Units of F/m are m s⁻² and stage distances have length units. Constant velocity in stage two agrees with zero resultant. SYNTHESIZE: When comparing two accelerated objects, equality of applied pushes is not enough to equate resultant forces. Create a small force ledger for each body: ΣF=F_push−F_resistance, then substitute mass times its measured acceleration. If a resistance is unknown, the measured acceleration determines the net force, so rearrange to infer the missing interaction. This is a constrained inverse calculation, not a proportional shortcut. Check both equations and compare with a limiting zero-resistance case. Different worked example: Two 2 kg carts have identical 8 N east pushes. One has no resistance and accelerates at 4 m s⁻²; the other has 2 N west resistance and accelerates at 3 m s⁻². Equal applied push did not produce equal net force. Independent check: If both resistances vanished, their equal masses and equal pushes would restore equal accelerations.

core1a.phenomenon: A person pushes a wall and feels the wall pushing back. The interaction is simultaneous; the two forces act on different bodies rather than canceling on one person.
core1a.scientific_narrative: Name the two interacting objects first. If A pushes B, B pushes A with equal magnitude and opposite direction in the same interaction. Draw the two arrows on different free-body diagrams. A single body's acceleration depends on all forces on that body and its mass; neither the equality of interaction forces nor different object masses forces equal acceleration. Additional Core1A operation bridges (AUTHOR CANDIDATE, not approved): REPRESENT: Every Newton-third-law statement needs two agents and two recipients. Write each force as 'force ON A BY B.' Put the B-on-A arrow only on A's free-body diagram and its counterpart A-on-B only on B's diagram. An arrow pointing opposite the first is not sufficient evidence of an interaction pair: two opposing forces on the same book (normal and gravity) are not each other's reactions. For combined systems, internal pairs may cancel in the total force ledger. Different worked example: When a hand pushes a door east with 8 N, show hand-on-door +8 N on the door drawing and door-on-hand −8 N on the hand drawing, not both on the door. Independent check: If another person pushes the door west with 5 N, that is a separate interaction and changes the door's net force; it does not change the first third-law pair's equality. JUSTIFY: A force pair has equal magnitude by the interaction law, but the two bodies can have different masses and other external forces. For an isolated two-object system, the internal pair contributes F and −F to the sum of forces, so the centre-of-mass acceleration is governed only by external force. Individual accelerations are obtained by dividing each body's own resultant by its own mass. Do not add action and reaction in a single-body equation, and do not infer equal accelerations from force equality. Different worked example: A 2 kg body receives 6 N east while its 3 kg partner receives 6 N west. Ignoring other forces, their accelerations have magnitudes 3 and 2 m s⁻² respectively; the mass-weighted acceleration sum is 2(3)+3(−2)=0. Independent check: Replacing either mass changes that body's acceleration without changing the equal-and-opposite pair for the stated contact force.

core1a.phenomenon: A box resting on a moving platform can accelerate although nobody pushes the box directly by hand. Its contact interactions change when we choose the box alone or the platform-plus-box as the system.
core1a.scientific_narrative: A free-body diagram represents forces acting *on the selected object*, not motion arrows or forces it exerts on others. State the system boundary first. On one box include gravity, support normal and any friction/tension acting on it; do not include its reaction on the support. For a combined multi-object system, internal contact forces cancel pairwise in the resultant, while external forces remain. Additional Core1A operation bridges (AUTHOR CANDIDATE, not approved): MODEL: For a group of bodies sharing motion, a combined-system diagram can eliminate internal interactions and reveal acceleration from external forces alone. Once acceleration is known, redraw a single-body diagram to recover the internal contact force needed to sustain that motion. The two equations are not competing answers: they answer different questions. Explicitly verify that a string remains taut or friction can sustain no slip before imposing common acceleration. Different worked example: A 1 kg upper box rests on a 2 kg sled; a 6 N east push accelerates both along a frictionless track. If no slip occurs, combined acceleration is 6/3=2 m s⁻², and the upper box requires 2 N east static friction. Independent check: On the lower sled, push minus the reaction friction equals 6−2=4 N, which is 2 kg×2 m s⁻². SYNTHESIZE: A common acceleration is an assumption to test, not a right earned by drawing the objects together. First calculate the acceleration they would share if no slipping occurred. Isolate the upper object to compute the horizontal contact force required. Compare that number against the maximum available static friction. If the inequality fails, discard the shared-acceleration model and use separate dynamics under an appropriate sliding-friction law. Do not hide the failed constraint by reporting the hypothetical acceleration as physical. Different worked example: A 1 kg box on a 3 kg platform under a 4 N push would need a=1 m s⁻² and 1 N upper-box friction. If the available limit is 2 N, shared acceleration is feasible; if the limit is 0.5 N, it is not. Independent check: For the feasible case, the platform equation 4−1=3 N equals 3 kg×1 m s⁻².

core1a.phenomenon: A gently pushed crate does not move, even though the push is nonzero. The contact surface supplies just enough static friction to oppose the tendency to slide, up to a maximum.
core1a.scientific_narrative: Before choosing a friction formula, inspect whether the two surfaces are stuck or sliding. For a stationary crate, horizontal force balance determines the *actual* static friction; the coefficient only supplies an upper bound. If the required friction exceeds the limit, the no-slip assumption fails. During sliding under a simple dry-friction model, kinetic friction has approximate magnitude μ_k N opposite the relative sliding direction. Additional Core1A operation bridges (AUTHOR CANDIDATE, not approved): MODEL: For a body that might remain stuck, compute the friction that *would* make the net tangential force zero. Static friction can take any necessary value within −μ_sN≤f_s≤+μ_sN; its limiting value is not always attained. If required magnitude exceeds that interval, static equilibrium is impossible and the contact must be reclassified. Once sliding, friction may be approximated as kinetic with magnitude μ_kN opposite relative slip, but only if μ_k and the normal force are actually supplied or justified. Different worked example: Two horizontal forces add to 5 N east while maximum static friction is 7 N. The crate can stay at rest with 5 N west friction, not automatically 7 N west. Independent check: At 8 N east tendency the required 8 N friction exceeds the 7 N limit, so the static model breaks. JUSTIFY: Static balance gives f_s=−(P−Q), where P is eastward and Q westward applied force. The condition |f_s|≤F_max becomes |P−Q|≤F_max. Solve both inequalities Q−F_max≤P≤Q+F_max; only then intersect with any physical restriction such as P≥0. The lower bound can matter because friction sometimes points east to oppose an excessive west pull. This inequality proof shows necessity (outside it no static solution) and sufficiency within the simplified dry-friction model. Different worked example: For a west pull Q=4 N, static limit F_max=6 N and east push P≥0, the rest interval is 0≤P≤10 N; at P=4 N actual friction is zero. Independent check: A push P=11 N requires 7 N west friction beyond the 6 N limit; a push P=0 needs 4 N east friction, which is available.

core1a.phenomenon: A block on a smooth ramp accelerates downslope even though gravity points vertically downward. The ramp's orientation changes the component of gravity along the allowed motion.
core1a.scientific_narrative: Choose axes parallel and perpendicular to the ramp, with upslope positive if a rope pulls up. The weight vector mg points vertically downward. For a ramp at angle θ above horizontal, its parallel magnitude is mg sinθ downward and perpendicular magnitude is mg cosθ into the ramp. A frictionless support cancels the perpendicular component while it remains in contact. Write the along-ramp resultant with signs before solving for a or a required tension. Additional Core1A operation bridges (AUTHOR CANDIDATE, not approved): REPRESENT: Draw weight mg vertically downward before introducing parallel and perpendicular axes. If the plane is at angle θ above horizontal, the component along the plane has magnitude mg sinθ down-slope and the into-plane component mg cosθ. With positive upslope and positive outward-normal directions, both gravity components are negative. For an ideal smooth plane with no normal acceleration and a rope parallel to the surface, the support is N=mg cosθ; it cannot pull the block into the surface. Different worked example: For a 2 kg block on a smooth 45° ramp with g=10 m s⁻², both gravity component magnitudes are 20/√2≈14.14 N. Downslope is negative if upslope positive, and normal support is +14.14 N outward. Independent check: At θ=0 the along-plane component vanishes and the normal component equals the full weight 20 N. SYNTHESIZE: For a rope pulling parallel to an inclined plane, the two applied tendencies along the surface are T upslope and mg sinθ downslope. To remain at rest, static friction must fill the signed difference: f_s=mg sinθ−T. That value can point either direction, so never pre-label friction as always upslope. Compare |mg sinθ−T| with the static limit; if exceeded, separate the sliding regime and supply a kinetic friction law. In a frictionless case the same signed sum gives acceleration directly. Different worked example: On a 30° plane with mg=20 N and static capacity 4 N, gravitational tendency downslope is 10 N. Rope tensions between 6 N and 14 N can be held in static equilibrium in the ideal model. Independent check: At T=10 N friction is zero, at T=14 N it is 4 N downslope, and at T=6 N it is 4 N upslope.

core1a.phenomenon: Two small carts connected by a light taut string accelerate together under a force on one cart. Cutting the string changes which forces act and removes the shared-acceleration constraint.
core1a.scientific_narrative: Before a cut, if a massless inextensible string is taut on a frictionless level track, both carts share acceleration along the string. Treat both as one system to find common acceleration from external force divided by total mass; then isolate a cart to find string tension. After cutting, tension vanishes; each cart obeys its own net-force equation. A cart without horizontal force preserves its velocity at the instant of cutting. Additional Core1A operation bridges (AUTHOR CANDIDATE, not approved): EXPLAIN: The force diagram for a taut-string system can change in an instant when a rope is cut or slackens. Before the event, the bodies may have a shared acceleration enforced by a tension constraint. Just after it, tension is absent and each external resultant changes. Under ordinary bounded forces over a vanishingly short cutting interval there is no impulse large enough to change velocity discontinuously, so each body retains its prior velocity at that instant while its acceleration may change immediately. If a rope snaps taut after slack motion, however, impulsive engagement needs a separate impact model; continuity cannot be assumed without examining it. Different worked example: A cart moving east at 3 m s⁻¹ is suddenly released from a pulling string on a smooth floor. Its acceleration becomes zero once tension vanishes, but it continues east at 3 m s⁻¹. Independent check: After 2 s coasting it travels another 6 m, rather than stopping at the cutting point. MODEL: A light rope transmits tension but cannot exert compression. Only when it is taut can two objects share the rope constraint, and an ideal massless inextensible connection then supplies a common acceleration along its own direction. Start with the separate free-body equations and the proposed common-acceleration constraint. Solve for tension and confirm T≥0, consistent rope geometry and initial velocities. A negative 'tension' means the taut-rope assumption is incompatible with the proposed motion and the model may need slack/separate dynamics. A sudden transition from slack to taut can require an impulse model. Different worked example: Two carts of 1 kg and 2 kg, connected by a taut rope on a smooth track, are pulled right with 6 N on the front cart. Shared a=6/3=2 m s⁻²; rope tension on the trailing 1 kg cart is 2 N, a valid positive pull. Independent check: On the front 2 kg cart, applied 6 N minus tension 2 N leaves 4 N, consistent with 2 kg×2 m s⁻².

progressive_examples.problem: A 2 kg and 3 kg cart are connected and pulled right with 10 N on a smooth horizontal track.
progressive_examples.reasoning: Both accelerate 10/(2+3)=2 m s⁻² right.

progressive_examples.problem: The 2 kg cart receives no horizontal force except string tension.
progressive_examples.reasoning: T=2 kg×2 m s⁻²=4 N right on the lighter cart.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Tension 4 N on 2 kg and opposing 4 N on B reconcile.

progressive_examples.problem: Cut the string while the 10 N force continues on the 3 kg cart.
progressive_examples.reasoning: Immediately after the cut: the 2 kg cart's acceleration becomes zero, while the 3 kg cart's becomes 10/3 m s⁻² right. Their velocities remain continuous at the cut.
progressive_examples.independent_check: After cut, tension vanishes but velocity has no impulsive jump.

figures.scene_description: Before the cut, a taut string constrains carts A and B to the same acceleration. After the cut there is no horizontal string force on either cart.

misconception.wrong_model: The 10 N external pull gives each cart an acceleration of 10/m, even while connected.
misconception.diagnostic: The taut rope constrains common acceleration; internal tension redistributes the external force between carts.
misconception.repair: Use the combined system first when the connection is taut, then choose one cart to recover the internal tension.

exit_check.task: Why is internal tension absent from the total system force equation but present in a single-cart equation?
exit_check.answer: Internal action-reaction tensions cancel in the total external resultant; on one cart the string is an external interaction that can accelerate it.
exit_check.reasoning: Immediately after cutting a tension of 4 N cannot persist. Recompute each horizontal resultant without rope force.

core1b.fresh_task: A 2 kg cart on a level low-friction track has 12 N east and 5 N west already acting. You may apply one additional horizontal force. Choose its direction and magnitude so that the cart accelerates at 1 m s⁻² west. Show the signed resultant equation and check it.
core1b.protected_work: Construct the missing applied force by reversing the usual resultant-to-acceleration calculation and preserving a signed direction.

stages.predict: If a cart is moving east but its required acceleration is west, must every force point west? State a prediction and reason.
stages.attempt: A 2 kg cart on a level low-friction track has 12 N east and 5 N west already acting. You may apply one additional horizontal force. Choose its direction and magnitude so that the cart accelerates at 1 m s⁻² west. Show the signed resultant equation and check it.
stages.reconstruct: Choose east positive. The desired resultant is m a = 2(−1)=−2 N. The known forces sum to +12−5=+7 N. Let the added force be F: 7+F=−2, so F=−9 N, or 9 N west. Check: 12−5−9=−2 N; dividing by 2 kg gives −1 m s⁻².
stages.diagnose: If you subtracted 12−5 and replied 7 N west, ask whether you found the existing resultant rather than the missing third force. If you used +2 N as the desired resultant, revisit the east-positive convention.
stages.repair: Write the target ΣF, the existing ΣF and the difference. Explain why the cart can still be moving east during westward acceleration.
stages.boundary_test: The same cart must instead continue at a constant eastward velocity. What additional horizontal force is required? Explain why speed is not the deciding input. Post-attempt boundary model: Constant velocity requires a_x=0 and ΣF_x=0. The known resultant is +7 N, so the added force must be 7 N west. Its current eastward velocity need not be zero.

core1b.fresh_task: A train and a loose toy initially move east together at 6 m s⁻¹. The train then accelerates east at a constant 2 m s⁻² for 2 s. The toy rests on a perfectly smooth horizontal shelf and experiences no horizontal force. Find the toy's velocity in the road frame and its displacement relative to the train at 2 s; state the direction of relative motion.
core1b.protected_work: Keep two ground-frame position models separate before subtracting them for relative displacement in the accelerating train.

stages.predict: Can an object move toward the rear of a speeding-up train without any horizontal force acting on it? Predict in the ground frame.
stages.attempt: A train and a loose toy initially move east together at 6 m s⁻¹. The train then accelerates east at a constant 2 m s⁻² for 2 s. The toy rests on a perfectly smooth horizontal shelf and experiences no horizontal force. Find the toy's velocity in the road frame and its displacement relative to the train at 2 s; state the direction of relative motion.
stages.reconstruct: Take east positive and x₀=0. Toy: x_toy=6t and v_toy=6 m s⁻¹ because ΣF=0. Train: x_train=6t+(1/2)(2)t²=6t+t². At t=2 s, toy travels 12 m and train 16 m, so x_toy−x_train=−4 m. The toy is 4 m toward the rear relative to the train, without a backward horizontal force.
stages.diagnose: If you give the toy acceleration +2 m s⁻², you have transferred the train's acceleration without a force. If you subtract speeds to claim a displacement, check the missing time integration.
stages.repair: List each object's horizontal force, ground acceleration and ground position equation. Only then compute the relative displacement.
stages.boundary_test: If the same train instead accelerates west at 2 m s⁻² for 2 s while still initially moving east, where is the toy relative to the train? Post-attempt boundary model: Toy displacement stays 12 m east. Train displacement is 6(2)+(1/2)(−2)(2²)=8 m east. The toy is 4 m ahead of the train; the sign of relative motion reverses.

core1b.fresh_task: Two carts on separate level tracks are each pushed east by the same applied force of 8 N. Cart A has mass 2 kg and measured acceleration 3 m s⁻² east; its constant westward resistance is unknown. Cart B experiences a measured 2 N westward resistance and accelerates at 1.5 m s⁻² east; its mass is unknown. Infer A's resistance and B's mass. State exactly why the resultant forces turn out to be equal, and independently verify both force equations.
core1b.protected_work: Distinguish applied from resultant forces; infer one resistance from measured acceleration, then recover the other mass and verify both independently.

stages.predict: Two carts have the same applied push but unknown or different resistances. Is it valid to equate their net forces before calculating both friction forces? Explain.
stages.attempt: Two carts on separate level tracks are each pushed east by the same applied force of 8 N. Cart A has mass 2 kg and measured acceleration 3 m s⁻² east; its constant westward resistance is unknown. Cart B experiences a measured 2 N westward resistance and accelerates at 1.5 m s⁻² east; its mass is unknown. Infer A's resistance and B's mass. State exactly why the resultant forces turn out to be equal, and independently verify both force equations.
stages.reconstruct: For A, ΣF_A=m_Aa_A=2×3=6 N east. Applied push is 8 N east, so the unknown A resistance is 8−6=2 N west. For B, the independently given resistance is 2 N west; hence ΣF_B=8−2=6 N east. Its mass is m_B=6/1.5=4 kg. The two net forces are equal only after checking the resistances. Verify A: 8−2=2×3=6 N; B: 8−2=4×1.5=6 N.
stages.diagnose: If you set the masses inversely proportional without checking A's unknown resistance, you equated applied pushes with resultants prematurely. If you found 8/1.5 kg, you omitted B's westward resistance.
stages.repair: Separate each cart's applied and resistant forces in two signed equations, solve the unknown A resistance and B mass, then check both left-to-right.
stages.boundary_test: B's westward resistance doubles from 2 N to 4 N while its mass remains 4 kg and the 8 N east push continues. What is B's new acceleration? Does the shared applied push now imply equal net force? Post-attempt boundary model: B now has resultant 8−4=4 N east and acceleration 4/4=1 m s⁻² east. A still has resultant 6 N and acceleration 3 m s⁻²; equal applied pushes no longer imply equal resultants.

core1b.fresh_task: Two carts A (4 kg) and B (1 kg) are in brief contact on a smooth horizontal track. A pushes B east with 12 N. An external actuator also pushes A east with 4 N, while another device pushes B west with 3 N. Identify the Newton-third-law contact pair (with each recipient labelled), calculate the instantaneous accelerations of A and B, then check the centre-of-mass acceleration from both the external resultant and the mass-weighted individual accelerations. Explain why the contact configuration may be transient.
core1b.protected_work: Separate action-reaction forces by recipient, add each body's external device, then reconcile body equations with the system centre of mass.

stages.predict: During a contact, can forces on different bodies be equal and opposite even while external actuators make the two accelerations very different? Label forces before calculating.
stages.attempt: Two carts A (4 kg) and B (1 kg) are in brief contact on a smooth horizontal track. A pushes B east with 12 N. An external actuator also pushes A east with 4 N, while another device pushes B west with 3 N. Identify the Newton-third-law contact pair (with each recipient labelled), calculate the instantaneous accelerations of A and B, then check the centre-of-mass acceleration from both the external resultant and the mass-weighted individual accelerations. Explain why the contact configuration may be transient.
stages.reconstruct: B-on-A contact =−12 N (west); A-on-B contact=+12 N (east). For A, ΣF_A=+4−12=−8 N, so a_A=−8/4=−2 m s⁻². For B, ΣF_B=+12−3=+9 N, so a_B=+9/1=+9 m s⁻². The combined system's external resultant is +4−3=+1 N, total mass 5 kg and a_CM=+1/5=+0.2 m s⁻². Independent check: (4×−2+1×9)/5=+0.2 m s⁻². The contact pair cancels only in the combined system; the opposing accelerations can cause separation soon after this instantaneous snapshot.
stages.diagnose: If you removed the 12 N contact arrow from each separate cart, you cancelled forces on different bodies. If you used 4−3−24 N as system resultant, you incorrectly counted the internal contact pair twice.
stages.repair: Draw two body-labelled force diagrams, then the combined-system diagram; explicitly compare the two independent centre-of-mass computations.
stages.boundary_test: At a moment when the same 12 N east contact force on B is still present, remove only B's 3 N west actuator. What is B's instantaneous acceleration and the combined-system centre-of-mass acceleration? Post-attempt boundary model: B then has +12 N net, so a_B=+12 m s⁻² east. Total external resultant becomes +4 N east on 5 kg, so a_CM=+0.8 m s⁻². The specified 12 N contact is instantaneous; whether contact persists requires a separate dynamical check.

core1b.fresh_task: A 1 kg box A rests without slipping on a 2 kg lower platform B. Both accelerate right at 2 m s⁻² on a level track. Only B is pushed directly from outside. Draw or describe the forces on A alone and determine the horizontal friction force on A, including direction. Explain why this force disappears from the horizontal force balance of the combined A+B system.
core1b.protected_work: Switch system boundaries to identify friction as the upper box's accelerating external force and the combined system's internal interaction.

stages.predict: A lower platform accelerates to the right. Can friction on a box resting on top point right as well? Predict and explain the contact tendency.
stages.attempt: A 1 kg box A rests without slipping on a 2 kg lower platform B. Both accelerate right at 2 m s⁻² on a level track. Only B is pushed directly from outside. Draw or describe the forces on A alone and determine the horizontal friction force on A, including direction. Explain why this force disappears from the horizontal force balance of the combined A+B system.
stages.reconstruct: Upper box A: weight 1g down, normal from B up, and static friction from B to the right. With horizontal acceleration +2 m s⁻², its only horizontal force is f_s=m_A a=1×2=2 N right. In A+B combined, B-on-A and A-on-B friction are equal opposite internal forces, so they cancel from the combined external horizontal resultant.
stages.diagnose: If you drew friction left because the system moves right, you assumed friction always opposes absolute motion. If you counted both friction arrows on A alone, you crossed the selected body boundary.
stages.repair: Write two lists: interactions on A, and interactions on A+B. Mark each force's two-object labels before solving.
stages.boundary_test: If the whole platform instead accelerates left at 2 m s⁻² with the box still not slipping, what direction and magnitude is friction on the upper box? Post-attempt boundary model: Its acceleration is left, so the only horizontal force on A is 2 N left. This is static friction from the platform opposing the tendency of A to lag behind the platform as it accelerates left.

core1b.fresh_task: A 2 kg crate initially rests on a level floor. Static friction can reach 6 N and, once it slides, kinetic friction has magnitude 4 N opposite its motion. An 8 N east push and a 3 N west rope pull act simultaneously. Determine whether the crate remains at rest and the actual static friction. The west rope pull then increases abruptly to 16 N while the east push remains 8 N. Determine whether static equilibrium remains possible; if it slips, find its initial acceleration with direction. State which contact model applies in each stage.
core1b.protected_work: Apply the static feasibility inequality before and after an external change, then switch to the stated kinetic friction model only if equilibrium fails.

stages.predict: Can a crate first remain stuck under opposing pulls and then slip in the opposite direction after one pull changes? Predict the role of the maximum static friction.
stages.attempt: A 2 kg crate initially rests on a level floor. Static friction can reach 6 N and, once it slides, kinetic friction has magnitude 4 N opposite its motion. An 8 N east push and a 3 N west rope pull act simultaneously. Determine whether the crate remains at rest and the actual static friction. The west rope pull then increases abruptly to 16 N while the east push remains 8 N. Determine whether static equilibrium remains possible; if it slips, find its initial acceleration with direction. State which contact model applies in each stage.
stages.reconstruct: Initially the nonfriction tendency is +8−3=+5 N east; static friction adjusts to −5 N (5 N west). Since |5|≤6 N, the crate remains at rest. With the rope raised to 16 N west, the nonfriction resultant is +8−16=−8 N (west); rest would require +8 N east static friction, exceeding its 6 N limit. The crate starts sliding west, so 4 N kinetic friction acts east. The actual net is +8−16+4=−4 N, and a=−4/2=−2 m s⁻², i.e. 2 m s⁻² west. Static limit is never substituted as actual kinetic friction.
stages.diagnose: If you answered 6 N for the initial static friction, you used maximum instead of actual. If you retained the 6 N static maximum during sliding, you failed to switch contact regimes.
stages.repair: Calculate each stage's signed nonfriction tendency; check the |f_s|≤6 N inequality before deciding which equation to use for acceleration.
stages.boundary_test: If the west rope pull instead becomes 14 N while the 8 N east push remains and the crate starts at rest, can it remain at rest and what friction acts? Post-attempt boundary model: The nonfriction tendency is 8−14=−6 N west; exactly +6 N east static friction can balance it. Rest remains possible at the limiting static contact, although any extra westward tendency would produce slip.

core1b.fresh_task: A 5 kg block is on a smooth 30° ramp. A rope parallel to the ramp pulls upslope; g=10 m s⁻². Determine the rope tension needed for 1 m s⁻² acceleration *upslope*. Give a signed along-ramp equation, state the contact assumptions, and check both the force and the resulting acceleration.
core1b.protected_work: Invert the along-slope resultant for the required upslope tension rather than just calculating gravity-driven downhill acceleration.

stages.predict: To accelerate a block uphill on a smooth ramp, must a rope pull with more or less than mg sinθ? Explain the sign.
stages.attempt: A 5 kg block is on a smooth 30° ramp. A rope parallel to the ramp pulls upslope; g=10 m s⁻². Determine the rope tension needed for 1 m s⁻² acceleration *upslope*. Give a signed along-ramp equation, state the contact assumptions, and check both the force and the resulting acceleration.
stages.reconstruct: Choose upslope positive. Gravity along the ramp =−mg sin30°=−25 N. The required net force for a=+1 m s⁻² is m a=+5 N. T−25=+5, so T=30 N upslope. Check: (30−25)/5=1 m s⁻². Perpendicular contact is N=5×10 cos30°≈43.3 N assuming rope parallel and no normal acceleration.
stages.diagnose: If you found 20 N, you subtracted the net-force requirement from gravity instead of adding it for uphill acceleration. If you used mg rather than mg sinθ you ignored axes.
stages.repair: Draw weight vertically, resolve mg sinθ downhill, and write T−mg sinθ=m a with declared upslope sign.
stages.boundary_test: The rope is suddenly cut while the block stays in contact with the smooth ramp. What is its subsequent acceleration, including direction? Is it necessarily already moving downhill? Post-attempt boundary model: With T=0, a=(0−25)/5=−5 m s⁻²: 5 m s⁻² downhill. If it had been moving uphill, it can still move uphill briefly while decelerating; acceleration direction alone does not fix velocity.

core1b.fresh_task: Two carts A=2 kg and B=3 kg move along a smooth horizontal track joined by a taut light string. A constant 15 N force pulls cart B rightward. Find their common acceleration before the string is cut. The string is then cut without an impulse while the same 15 N continues on B. Find the immediate accelerations of A and B after cutting, and state what happens to their velocities at the instant of the cut.
core1b.protected_work: Recognize the change of system and contact constraint at the cut, separating acceleration updates from continuous velocity.

stages.predict: If a string joining two speeding-up carts is cut, does the unpulled cart instantly stop? Predict its velocity and acceleration just after cutting.
stages.attempt: Two carts A=2 kg and B=3 kg move along a smooth horizontal track joined by a taut light string. A constant 15 N force pulls cart B rightward. Find their common acceleration before the string is cut. The string is then cut without an impulse while the same 15 N continues on B. Find the immediate accelerations of A and B after cutting, and state what happens to their velocities at the instant of the cut.
stages.reconstruct: Before cutting, total mass=2+3=5 kg, so a_common=15/5=3 m s⁻² right. After cutting, A has no horizontal force, so a_A=0; B has 15 N right on 3 kg, so a_B=5 m s⁻² right. Without an impulse, both keep the velocity they had at the cutting instant, but B then increases its speed faster while A coasts.
stages.diagnose: If A stops immediately, velocity and acceleration have been conflated. If both still accelerate at 3 m s⁻², you carried the rope constraint beyond its actual physical existence.
stages.repair: Draw two time intervals, mark which external forces and constraints exist in each, and state position/velocity continuity across a non-impulsive cut.
stages.boundary_test: Suppose the string had been slack from the start, with B pulled at 15 N and A initially moving right at 2 m s⁻¹. What are the initial accelerations of A and B? Post-attempt boundary model: Without a taut connection, A's horizontal net force is zero, so its acceleration is zero and it coasts at 2 m s⁻¹. B's acceleration is 15/3=5 m s⁻² right. The combined 5 kg formula is invalid from the start.

stages.attempt: Two blocks A=2 kg and B=3 kg lie on the same smooth 30° ramp (g=10 m s⁻²) connected by a taut light rope. An external 25 N upslope force pulls B; the system is initially moving upslope at 2 m s⁻¹ and the rope remains taut. Find acceleration and rope tension before a non-impulsive cut. Immediately after the cut the same external pull still acts on B but no rope force acts on A. Find both accelerations and determine their separation increase 2 s after the cut, assuming no collision and both continue on the ramp. Explain why acceleration direction does not fix immediate velocity direction.
stages.reconstruct: Upslope positive. Total downslope gravity=(2+3)(10)(0.5)=25 N; external upslope pull25 N gives combined ΣF=0 and shared acceleration0; initial 2 m s⁻¹ upslope persists before cut. For A alone: T−(2×10×0.5)=0, hence T=10 N upslope. After cut A has a_A=−10/2=−5 m s⁻² downslope; B has a_B=(25−3×10×0.5)/3=+10/3 m s⁻² upslope. Both velocities at instant of cut stay +2 m s⁻¹, but their relative acceleration is 10/3−(−5)=25/3 m s⁻². Starting from zero relative separation/velocity at cutting, after 2 s separation increase =0.5(25/3)(2²)=50/3≈16.67 m, with B moving farther upslope.

stages.predict: Can a two-block trolley accelerate under an external pull while the upper block remains stuck? Predict how the static-friction limit constrains pull strength.
stages.attempt: A 2 kg top block rests on a 3 kg lower platform on a frictionless horizontal track. The two blocks share motion while no slipping occurs; friction between them has maximum magnitude 5 N. An external adjustable eastward force F≥0 acts only on the lower platform. Derive the full allowable interval of F for no-slip acceleration, proving why the internal friction forces cancel for the combined system but still accelerate the upper block. Include the F=0 coasting case and test F=15 N.
stages.reconstruct: For both bodies, internal static-friction pair cancels, so a=F/(2+3)=F/5 east. On top block alone, its only horizontal force is friction f=2a=2F/5 east. The equal-opposite top-on-platform friction is 2F/5 west; they cancel only when both are inside the chosen system. No slip requires |f|≤5 N, giving 2F/5≤5, so 0≤F≤12.5 N. At F=0, net force and a=0 yet the pair can coast with any existing constant velocity. At F=15 N the required f=6 N exceeds the 5 N limit, so no-slip assumption fails; use a slipping model.
